lesson.grammar_point: modals of certainty and obligation for investment risk

listenings.text: When I rate a toll road, I do not start with the engineering. I start with three questions. First, how likely is the traffic forecast? Most forecasts are too optimistic, so I usually reduce them by twenty percent. Second, who has to pay if the costs go up? If the contract is clear, the risk is lower. If nobody knows, the concessionaire will probably pay, and that must affect the rating. Third, can the government change the tariff? In some countries, that is very unlikely. In others, it may happen before every election. The answer to those three questions decides most of the rating.

Good morning, everybody. Here is our risk update for the quarter. The good news is that none of our projects is close to a default. Traffic on the two toll roads is higher than we expected, and both concessionaires are creditworthy. The bad news is the currency. The dollar went up eight percent, and if it continues, our returns are likely to fall next year. We have to be honest about that. We are not going to sell anything in a panic. But we may need to hedge a larger part of the debt, and we will decide that at the next board meeting in March.

paras: Every infrastructure project has risks: construction can be late, traffic can be lower than expected, and a new government may change the rules. Investors know this. What they really want to understand is how likely each risk is, and who has to pay if it happens. A toll road with a strong contract and a creditworthy concessionaire can attract money at a low cost. The same road with unclear rules may not attract any money at all.

In emerging markets, two risks usually decide the price. The first is the currency risk. A project that earns in reais but borrows in dollars must be very careful, because volatility in the exchange rate can turn a good return into a loss in a few months. The second is regulatory risk. Investors look at the history of a country: if contracts have been respected for twenty years, a sudden change is unlikely to happen. If not, they ask for a higher return, more collateral or a guarantee from a development bank.

Good lawyers and managers do not promise that there is no risk. They explain the worst-case scenario, show how the contract will mitigate it, and say clearly what each party has to do. For a rating agency, that clarity is worth a lot. Experts say that a well-written contract can improve the rating of a project, and a better rating is likely to reduce the cost of the loan for everybody, including the users who pay the tariff.
